## 8. Models

### Sticker (`lumenary:sticker`, models this process)

_From: Self-adhesive labels and street culture; when: 1935 label, 1980s vinyl stickers; works best on: One subject on a plain, different-coloured background._

A die-cut sticker is recognised by its edge. The artwork is cut out along its own outline, a margin of white vinyl is left all round so the cut never touches the ink, and the whole thing sits a hair above the surface. Flat colour and a dark keyline come from the printing. Gloss and a lifting corner come from the plastic.

**How it is made, as the model does it:**

1. Guess the subject from how unlike the frame’s border each pixel is, and keep the largest patch.
2. Redraw the picture in flat cartoon colour with ink lines.
3. Grow the subject’s shape outward and round it off to make the white border.
4. Add a dark keyline where artwork meets border, and a slanted band of gloss.
5. Fold one corner back in a mirror line and show its grey underside.
6. Place it on a coloured surface with a soft shadow.

**The maths:**

$$\text{score}=0.8\,\operatorname{clamp}\!\Big(\frac{\lVert C-C_{\text{edge}}\rVert_{1}}{300}\Big)+0.2\,\big(1-\operatorname{clamp}(u^{2}+v^{2})\big)$$

_How likely a pixel is to be subject: distance of its colour C from the border’s average, and closeness to the centre (u, v from −1 to 1)._ (written for this model: specific)

$$\text{border}=S_{0.035,\,0.075}\!\Big(B_{b}^{2}\,B_{4}^{2}\,M\Big)$$

_The sticker’s outline: the mask M blurred, then blurred again by the border width b, and cut at a low level._ (primitives: dilate, blur)

$$(x,\ y)\ \mapsto\ (c-y,\ c-x)$$

_The peel: reflection in the fold line x + y = c._ (primitives: coordinate-warp)

**Dials:** `shape` (Cut) = "auto" (auto, circle, square, badge); `cut` (How much is subject) = 50 [0 to 100]; `border` (White border) = 55 [10 to 100]; `colours` (Colours) = 10 [5 to 16]; `lines` (Ink lines) = 55 [0 to 100]; `gloss` (Gloss) = 55 [0 to 100]; `peel` (Peeling corner) = true; `back` (Behind it) = "mint" (mint, pink, yellow, sky, desk, slate).

**History:** R. Stanton Avery built the first machine for self-adhesive labels in Los Angeles in 1935. Bumper stickers followed in the 1940s. Printed vinyl and computer-driven cutting plotters made custom shapes cheap in the 1980s, and stickers became part of skateboarding and street art. Messaging apps turned them digital around 2011, when large sticker sets joined the emoji.
